Devant l’entrée du métro Jean-Talon, Éri: At the entrance to the Jean-Talon metro station, Éric stands holding out an empty coffee cup to passersby. Smiling broadly, the 55-year-old isn't bothered by the cold of this stormy winter day. The force of the wind doesn't seem to intimidate him either. “At least in front of the [metro] door, I say hello to people; people talk to me, regulars come see me every day. I see them. That's nice, at least,” he says.
Éric est en situation d’itinérance depui: Éric has been homeless for two years. Before that, he worked for about twenty years as a labourer at an electric company and lived on the first floor of a duplex owned by his grandmother. But a series of incidents left him without a fixed address.
« J’ai d’abord perdu mon emploi et j’ai: “First I lost my job, and then I was diagnosed with manic depression,” he confides. After several months of searching for work in vain, Éric gave up. “I was discouraged. After they kept me in the hospital for eight months at Louis-H. Lafontaine, I had no strength, not even the will to look for a job.”
Le duplex où réside à cette époque Éric: The duplex where Éric was living at the time was soon put up for sale by his family, leaving him without a home and alone in the face of an invisible mental illness. “The new owner put me out because that was the deal. I looked for an apartment. Nothing. I ended up on the street,” he tells us in a detached tone.
Aujourd’hui, la santé mentale d’Éric s’e: Today, Éric's mental health has improved, though he is still considered depressed. He gets only one appointment a month with a psychiatrist. The doctor listens to him talk about “whatever comes to mind” and prescribes medication. “A psychiatrist gives you meds, and once you're stabilized, that's good enough for them. You're taken care of, you know,” he concludes offhandedly.

Le cas d’Éric n’est pas isolé. D’après l: Éric's case is not isolated. According to the ministère de la Santé et des Services sociaux (MSSS), <l1>30% to 50%</l1> of people experiencing homelessness in Quebec are believed to have mental health problems.
À seulement 15 ans, Jayne Malenfant a dû: At just 15, Jayne Malenfant had to leave her community of Kapuskasing, Ontario, to find mental health support. “There weren't many services in Kapuskasing. So it was really a choice between staying with my family or accessing mental health support.” It was the need to stay close to her psychologist that led her to spend three years homeless in Saskatoon.
Ce qui a sauvé Jayne, c’est le soutien d: What saved Jayne was the support of her community: friends and family members took turns housing her. “What helped me was having stable people around me. It wasn't government services. When you're homeless, you can't count on social services to get out of it,” she insists.

Aujourd’hui, Jayne Malenfant est experte: Today, Jayne Malenfant is an expert on youth homelessness and a professor at McGill University. In her view, the mental health of homeless people is addressed too late. The mental disorders that people experiencing homelessness suffer from often stem from the precarious conditions they live in, or are frequently made worse by them. When left untreated, these disorders can lead to psychotic crises. “Very often, it's only during moments of psychotic crisis that a homeless person's situation is considered: that's true for mental health, but also for a housing solution,” says M<sup>s</sup>. Malenfant.

And sometimes, the response to these crises is not medical but judicial: “When you're homeless, psychotic crises are much more visible than if you have one at home. So often, the response to these homeless people in crisis isn't one of support: it's the police who intervene.”
C’est ce qu’a vécu Alain Magloire le 3 f: That is what Alain Magloire experienced on February 3, 2014. A father of two with a bachelor's degree in molecular biology from UQAM, Mr. Magloire suffered from mental illness. After becoming homeless, the microbiologist <l1>was not receiving adequate medical follow-up</l1>. In the middle of a psychotic crisis, he was shot dead in broad daylight by Service de police de la Ville de Montréal officers after displaying violent behaviour. Alain Magloire might have avoided a tragic end had he been in a shelter at the time of his psychotic crisis.
Parmi les refuges, il existe ceux qui of: Among shelters, some offer services 24 hours a day, and others are open only during the day. Known as “day centres,” these shelters provide resources during the day, such as meals, showers, clean clothes and other supports. Shelters open 24 hours a day offer, in addition to these services, a place to stay overnight, often during the coldest months of the year. Éric remains skeptical about these solutions, however. In his view, these shelters don't meet everyone's needs.

Chaque mois, un travailleur social vient: Every month, a social worker visits Éric to hand over the $820 in last-resort financial assistance he receives from the government. Because he has no permanent address, he can't open a bank account. “A nice sum,” he says, but one that still doesn't allow him to find affordable housing. “You know how much a 1½ costs? 900 bucks! I'd like to find a place for $800 at least, I've been looking for a year and a half!” he says, bewildered.
Depuis quelques mois, le quinquagénaire: For the past few months, the man in his fifties has been staying at an emergency shelter in the Villeray neighbourhood. He also spends time on street corners when he has to give up his spot for seven days. Indeed, like the Refuge du Cœur de l’Île, some emergency shelters in Montréal give homeless people a bed for 14 days, after which the person must leave the shelter for seven days to make room for others. Still, in an amused tone, Éric tells us he prefers the street to the shelter: “The shelter is rough. There's coughing, farting, stinking, shouting. It's a free-for-all. I'd rather sleep outside.”
La dépression d’Éric rend la cohabitatio: Éric's depression makes living alongside others difficult. “Their mental condition makes them flip out,” he admits. But what he finds hardest is the loneliness he lives with every day. He keeps his distance from others to avoid bad company. Drugs and alcohol are commonplace in some circles.
« La solitude, c’est dur. C’est vraiment: “Loneliness is hard. It's really hard. But in these environments, it's better to be alone,” he says pensively.

Katherine McIntosh, directrice générale: Katherine McIntosh, executive director of the Refuge du Cœur de l’Île, and Émile Bernier, site coordinator, lament the lack of resources to care for people with mental disorders, such as Éric.
« Sans exagérer – et c’est en concordanc: “Without exaggerating – and this matches my experience as a former outreach worker and street worker – I feel like 80% of the people experiencing homelessness here have mental health disorders, but you can never tell apart those with mental health issues from those who use and the others,” says Émile Bernier. Although he is aware of the mental health problems each homeless person may be experiencing, the coordinator reminds us that he is not in a position to diagnose people arriving at the shelter: “We can't diagnose these people; we're not health professionals.”

En attendant, le Refuge du Cœur de l’Île: In the meantime, the Refuge du Cœur de l’Île works with an outreach team associated with the CIUSSS du Nord-de-l’Île-de-Montréal, which includes a psychiatrist. However, the psychiatrist only sees people experiencing uncontrolled psychosis. “To look after the 80% of people who have mental disorders, we'd need 15 psychologists, plus two or three more psychiatrists. But our current psychiatrist has no choice but to focus only on those people with uncontrolled psychotic disorders,” says Mr. Bernier. This is nonetheless seen as a victory by the site coordinator, because “some people have trouble getting follow-ups in institutions.” “Now, at least, there's a psychiatrist who comes here, and when residents agree, it's easier to start follow-ups,” he explains.

The shelter is limited to 45 places to make sure it can offer three meals a day to its residents. And when the shelter is full, government funding only covers extra chairs on which people can lie down.

Like the Refuge du Cœur de l’Île, Résilience Montréal lacks the resources to support people with mental disorders. “The majority of people who come to use our services here have obvious mental health problems,” says David Chapman, the organization's founder and executive director. “When it comes to the help they need, there's a big gap, and we're trying to fill that gap by providing them with care. But for that, more funds would need to go to emergency services.”
Lorsqu’on demande à Katherine McIntosh q: When asked what solutions could ensure better care for homeless people living with invisible mental disorders, Katherine McIntosh's answer is direct: “The solution is Housing First: giving people apartments and following up in those apartments to make sure they readapt to social life and improve their living conditions.”
Au Québec, l’approche<l1>Logement d’abor: In Quebec, the <l1>Housing First</l1> approach gives people experiencing homelessness the chance to have housing whose cost is set at 30% of the social assistance they receive. The initiative aims to give these people a stable place from which they can then access mental or physical health care, job search support, or assistance for people dependent on drugs. Access to these programs remains difficult, however, explains youth homelessness expert Jayne Malenfant, notably because of the housing crisis affecting Montréal.
En Finlande, une <l1>approche de type Lo: In Finland, a <l1>Housing First–style approach</l1> seems to be working. Every year, the government invests $45 million to build or renovate social housing for homeless people. Often cited in Europe as an example to follow, the country has recorded a drop in the number of homeless people, from 18,000 in 1987 to 7,000 in 2016. The Housing First–style strategy has put Finland among the few Western countries where homelessness is steadily declining. The country hopes to resolve this social problem for good by 2027.
Au Québec, le nombre de sans-abri ne ces: In Quebec, the number of homeless people keeps rising. The latest census, made public in September 2023, reports 10,000 people experiencing visible homelessness during 2022, including 4,690 in Montréal. During 2023, fewer than <l1>5,000 affordable and social housing units were built in Quebec.</l1>
Nous avons sollicité des clarifications: We asked the ministère de la Santé et des Services sociaux (MSSS) and the ministère des Affaires municipales et de l’Habitation (MAMH) for clarification on the obstacles to building social housing, but had received no response at the time of publication.

Lord, spécialiste de l’aménagem: According to Mr. Lord, a land-use planning specialist, the complexity surrounding the construction of social housing in Quebec is tied to the structure of government. “Unlike Finnish cities, Quebec cities have neither the mandate nor the funds for housing construction.” In Quebec, each city issues calls for projects to community organizations to start the housing construction process. However, reviewing and then approving these projects involves long delays. “Between submitting the project to the Société d’habitation du Québec (SHQ) and handing the keys to residents, five to ten years can go by,” Mr. Lord explains.

Privilégier le financement de l’approche: Prioritizing funding for the Housing First approach over funding for shelters is not a solution, Mr. Chapman insists. “If there's no adequate emergency services program and no safe place where people can go while waiting for housing, we'll end up with deaths,” he laments. A story he doesn't want to see repeated. In 2022, an investigation by Le Devoir revealed that some forty homeless people had been found dead over the course of the year.
